9.10 Stratification for a Survey Variable with Cauchy Distribution

If the study variable follows the Cauchy distribution on the interval \([y_{0}, y_{L}]\), its two-parameter probability density function is given by:

\[\begin{eqnarray} f(y; \mu, \sigma)=\dfrac{1}{{\pi}\sigma\left[1+\left(\dfrac{y-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2\right]} \;\;\;\;-\infty < y < +\infty \tag{50} \end{eqnarray}\]

where \(\mu\) is the location parameter which specifies the location of the peak of the distribution and \(\sigma\) is the scale parameter, which specifies the half-width at half maximum of the distribution.

9.10.1 DP Solution for Cauchy Distribution

To solve the MPP formulated for Cauchy distribution (50), we apply the algorithm using the DP technique discussed in Section 4. The recurrence relations used to determine the OSB are given by:

For the first stage, \(k=1\), at \(l_{1}^{*}=d_{1}\):

\[\begin{eqnarray} \Phi_{1}d_{1}&=& \textrm{Sqrt}\Biggl\{\dfrac{1}{\pi^{2}}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{1}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]\nonumber\\[10pt] &&\times\left[\mu\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{1}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)+\left(\mu^2-\sigma^2\right)\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{1}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right.\nonumber\\[10pt] &&+\sigma\left(d_{1}+y_{0}\right)-\mu\sigma\ln\left(\left(y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left.\left(\mu^2-\sigma^2\right)\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\sigma y_{0}\right]\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left[\dfrac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\left[\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{1}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)+2\mu\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{1}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right.\right.\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left.\left.\sigma\ln\left(\left(y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)-2\mu\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]\right]^{2}\Biggr\} \tag{51} \end{eqnarray}\]

And for the stages \(k\geq2\):

\[\begin{eqnarray} \Phi_{k}d_{k}&=&\min_{0\leq l_{k}\leq d_{k}}\Biggl\{ \textrm{Sqrt}\Biggl\{ \dfrac{1}{\pi^{2}}\left[\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}-l_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]\nonumber\\[10pt] &&\times\left[\mu\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{k}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)+\left(\mu^2-\sigma^2\right)\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right.\nonumber\\[10pt] &&+\sigma\left(d_{k}+y_{0}\right)-\mu\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{k}-l_{k}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left.\left(\mu^2-\sigma^2\right)\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}-l_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)-\sigma y_{h-1}\right]\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left[\dfrac{1}{4\pi^{2}}\left[\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{k}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)+2\mu\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right.\right.\nonumber\\[10pt] &&-\left.\left.\sigma\ln\left(\left(d_{k}-l_{k}+y_{0}-\mu\right)^2+\sigma^2\right)-2\mu\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{d_{k}-l_{k}+y_{0}-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\right]\right]^{2} \Biggr\} + \Phi_{k-1}(d_{k}-l_{k})\Biggr\}. \tag{52} \end{eqnarray}\]

Substituting the values of \(\mu\), \(\sigma\), \(y_{0}\) and \(d\), the OSW (\(l_{h}^{*}\)) and the OSB (\(y_{h}^{*}=y_{h-1}^{*}-l_{h}^{*}\)) are obtained by executing the strata.data() function.

9.10.2 A Numerical Example for Cauchy Distribution

The Boston data from the MASS package is used to demonstrate the application for Cauchy population. In this example, the variable ‘black’ is used since it exhibits a 2-parameter Cauchy distribution with the location and scale parameters as \(location = 393.864307\) and \(scale = 4.710457\) respectively. The minimum and maximum values are \([y_{0}, y_{L}] = [0.32, 396.9]\), which implies that \(d=396.58\).

black = Boston$black
hist(black)

min(black); max(black); d=max(black)-min(black);d

#> [1] 396.9

fit <- fitdist(black, distr="cauchy", method="mle")
fit

When the data include negative values, as they can for a Cauchy variable, the families that are defined only for positive values cannot be fitted. The package skips them quietly and chooses among the remaining families by AIC.

Similarly, in order to find the OSB and other quantities, we can apply the strata.distr() function to a Cauchy population. Based on the assumption from past knowledge that the population follows Cauchy distribution with the given attributes such as the initial value, distance, parameters, etc., we can execute the following command to obtain the results:

#for a cauchy distribution with initial value of x0=-1, d=2 and 
#location and scale parameters 0 and 1 respectively
res <- strata.distr(h=2, initval=-1, dist=2, distr = "cauchy",
             params = c(location=0, scale=1), n=500, N=5000)
#> The program is running, it'll take some time!
summary(res)

10 Summary of Method Comparison Across All Supported Distributions

To compare the four solvers on the examples of Section 9, we ran strata.data() with \(h = 3\) on the data used in each distribution section. Table 1 shows the objective function \(\sum W_h S_h\) (WhShTot) for each solver, and the gap of the DP cost above the exact optimum. The values were computed with stratifyR 2.0-3; the code to reproduce them is given after the table.

Table 1: Objective function (WhShTot) of the four solvers with h = 3 on the examples of Section 9. ‘AIC family’ is the distribution chosen by AIC, which the DP optimises. ‘DP gap’ is the DP cost above the exact optimum. Lower WhShTot means a more efficient design.
Section Data N AIC family DP COBYLA GLOBAL EXACT DP gap (%)
Pareto Simulated 5000 pareto 0.92760 0.92710 0.92710 0.92710 0.05
Triangular math final marks 487 weibull 7.11720 7.09160 7.09160 7.09160 0.36
Right-triangular Simulated 1000 rtriangle 0.48890 0.48850 0.48850 0.48850 0.08
Weibull anaemia Iron 724 norm 2.46380 2.44340 2.44340 2.44340 0.84
Gamma anaemia Folate 724 norm 2.93570 2.89850 2.89850 2.89850 1.28
Exponential Simulated 5000 exp 0.27360 0.27341 0.27341 0.27341 0.07
Uniform Simulated 5000 unif 1.24710 1.24700 1.24700 1.24700 0.01
Normal Simulated 5000 norm 0.71698 0.71685 0.71685 0.71685 0.02
Log-normal hies Expenditure 3566 lnorm 4678.50000 4598.90000 4598.90000 4598.90000 1.73
Cauchy Boston black 506 cauchy 20.67200 14.92100 14.92100 14.92100 38.50

Three points stand out.

  1. COBYLA, GLOBAL and EXACT agree everywhere. On all ten examples, the two fast solvers found the exact optimum. Each of the three took at most a few seconds.

  2. DP is within 2% of the optimum when the fitted model is reasonable. The gap is below 0.1% for the Pareto, right-triangular, exponential, uniform and normal data, where the chosen family matches the data well, and between 0.4% and 1.7% for the other skewed examples. The DP took 20 to 50 seconds per run at \(h = 3\).

  3. The DP depends on the fitted model. For the Boston black variable, the AIC chooses the Cauchy, but the data are strongly skewed to the left and the fitted Cauchy describes them poorly. The DP boundaries, which are optimal for that model, cost 38.5% more than the exact optimum for the actual data. Fitting a distribution is what makes strata.distr() possible when no data are available, but when the data are at hand, it is worth checking the DP result against method = "exact".

Note that the family chosen by AIC can differ from the section name. For example, the Iron and Folate data (with the minimum replaced as in Section 9) are fitted best by the normal. The family chosen, and therefore the DP result, can also differ slightly between platforms when a maximum-likelihood fit is close to failing. The COBYLA, GLOBAL and EXACT results do not depend on the fit.

In summary, "exact" gives the best design for a given population, "cobyla" gives the same answer in almost all cases and is the fastest, and "dp" remains the default because it optimises a smooth fitted model and is the method of the original package.

The table can be reproduced with the following code (it takes a few minutes because of the DP runs):

library(MASS); library(triangle); library(actuar)
pops <- list()
set.seed(8235411); pops$Pareto <- actuar::rpareto(5000, shape=5, scale=8)
data(math); pops$Triangular <- math$final_marks
set.seed(12546); pops$`Right-triangular` <- rtriangle(n=1000, a=2, b=8, c=2)
data(anaemia)
x <- anaemia$Iron;   x[x == min(x)] <- -0.001; pops$Weibull <- x
x <- anaemia$Folate; x[x == min(x)] <- -0.001; pops$Gamma   <- x
set.seed(28951); pops$Exponential <- rexp(5000, rate=1.36)
set.seed(15669); pops$Uniform <- runif(5000, min=2, max=15)
set.seed(89821); pops$Normal <- rnorm(5000, mean=16, sd=1.65)
data(hies); pops$`Log-normal` <- hies$Expenditure
pops$Cauchy <- Boston$black

tab <- t(sapply(pops, function(d) {
  n <- min(500, floor(length(d) / 2))
  sapply(c("dp", "cobyla", "global", "exact"),
         function(m) objective(strata.data(d, h=3, n=n, method=m)))
}))
tab
